lead: Turmeric root extract is a preparation made from the rhizome of Curcuma longa, a plant of the ginger family. Its main coloured constituent is curcumin, a yellow polyphenol that is also used as a food colouring, a dietary supplement ingredient and a cosmetic ingredient [1][6]. In skincare it is marketed mainly as a brightening or antioxidant ingredient, a use that echoes the long tradition in South Asia of applying turmeric paste to the skin, notably in pre-wedding haldi ceremonies [6].

Laboratory work has examined curcumin and turmeric extract in skin-cell models, for example a 2023 cell-culture study combining turmeric root extract with another antioxidant in keratinocytes exposed to ultraviolet light [2]. No clinical trial of topical turmeric root extract for skin brightening or complexion has been published. Wikipedia's curcumin article states that extensive studies have not established a medical value for curcumin, citing its instability and poor absorption, and also lists it as a contact allergen [1].

Turmeric root extract also appears in oral supplements, where it is combined with ingredients such as glucosamine and boswellia in joint formulas [3][7]. Those uses concern joint comfort and general wellness rather than skin.

angle.text: Turmeric root extract is used in brightening and antioxidant skincare products with the aim of a more even, radiant complexion. The idea rests on curcumin's antioxidant behaviour in cell studies and on traditional use of turmeric on skin.

paras: Turmeric is the ground or extracted root of Curcuma longa, a perennial herb native to the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia whose rhizomes are yellow-orange and aromatic [6]. Curcumin is a diarylheptanoid polyphenol that dissolves poorly in water but readily in organic solvents, and it binds metal ions such as iron and copper [1]. Extracts are sold for culinary use, as supplements and as cosmetic ingredients, and also appear in combination products, including joint supplements listed on US drug-label databases [3].

Turmeric has been used in Asia for centuries, first as a dye and later in folk medicine, and it appears in Ayurveda, Siddha, traditional Chinese medicine and Unani. Archaeological and textual evidence of its use ranges from sites dated to about 2600 to 2200 BCE to Assyrian texts of the seventh century BCE, and medieval Europeans called it Indian saffron [6]. In India many Hindu communities apply turmeric paste to the bride and groom before weddings in haldi ceremonies, and in Bengal the equivalent is the gaye holud [6].

Chemists Vogel and Pelletier first isolated a yellow colouring matter from the rhizome in 1815, and in 1910 Miłobędzka and Lampe proposed the structure of curcumin as diferuloylmethane, with a synthesis following in 1913 [1].

Product listings describe turmeric root extract as a skin-brightening ingredient, often alongside other plant extracts. Curcumin is used in cosmetics as a colorant and an active, and the cell data on antioxidant defences in keratinocytes are the usual scientific reference for the claim [2][1]. No published human data show whether topical use changes skin tone or pigmentation.

Curcumin is chemically unstable and poorly soluble in water, and little of an oral dose reaches the bloodstream because it is extensively metabolised and mostly excreted unchanged [1]. Medicinal chemists describe it as a pan-assay interference compound because it gives positive results in many laboratory assays, which complicates interpretation of in vitro findings [1].

In the 2023 keratinocyte study, turmeric root extract combined with dimethylmethoxy chromanol, a synthetic analogue of gamma-tocopherol, reduced ultraviolet-induced oxidative damage and increased endogenous antioxidant enzymes such as NQO1 and superoxide dismutase [2].

No studies found for topical turmeric root extract as a skin-brightening or cosmetic agent. Related laboratory research is limited to cell models: curcumin suppressed TGF-beta signaling in fibroblasts taken from scleroderma patients [4], and a combination of turmeric root extract and dimethylmethoxy chromanol reduced ultraviolet-induced oxidative damage in a human keratinocyte line [2]. These cell studies did not test skin brightening in people.

Human trials of oral turmeric root extract concern other topics. A double-blind crossover study in twelve older adults examined cerebral oxygenation after turmeric root extract during handgrip exercise [8], a 2024 study looked at skeletal muscle oxygen saturation in older participants taking 10 g of turmeric root extract [9], and an eight-week placebo-controlled community trial tested a joint supplement that included turmeric among its ingredients [10]. A 1999 placebo-controlled trial studied a celandine and turmeric extract for upper abdominal pain from biliary dyskinesia [11]. Registered trials include turmeric extract and oxidative stress in 44 Muay Thai athletes and sedentary men [12] and turmeric and exercise-induced muscle damage in 53 participants [13].

Wikipedia reports that curcumin is a contact allergen, may interact with prescription drugs, and that reported oral side effects include nausea, diarrhoea, hives and dizziness; it also records cases of liver injury linked to curcumin supplements [1]. A 2015 case report described yellow discolouration of the soles in a patient who took one capsule of turmeric root extract daily for four months, which faded after she stopped [5]. Curcumin is a strong yellow pigment, and staining of skin or fabric is a recognised property of the compound.
Turmeric as a spice has also been adulterated with lead-containing colourants such as lead chromate; the US FDA issued import alerts on turmeric from India and Bangladesh between 2013 and 2019 [6].

Turmeric is an approved food colouring in the EU (E100), under WHO listing and by the US FDA [1][6]. The FDA issued warning letters to supplement makers between 2018 and 2023 over claims that products treat disease [1]. In 2019 the European Medicines Agency accepted traditional use of turmeric for mild digestive complaints but found insufficient evidence of efficacy [6].

name: Turmeric root extract

card.summary: Curcumin-rich plant extract sold as a skin brightener; evidence for that use is limited to cell studies.
card.note: Contact allergen; strongly pigmented and can stain.

quick.overview:
Turmeric root extract comes from the Curcuma longa rhizome and is used in cosmetics as a brightening and antioxidant ingredient. Its main pigment is curcumin.
No human trials of topical turmeric extract for skin tone have been published. Research is limited to cell-culture experiments.
quick.mechanism: In laboratory cell models curcumin has been reported to dampen TGF-beta signaling and, combined with another antioxidant, to reduce UV-induced oxidative damage in keratinocytes. Whether this translates to visible brightening in people has not been tested.
quick.risks: Curcumin is listed as a contact allergen and a strong yellow pigment. Oral use has been linked to side effects such as nausea and, rarely, liver injury, and a case report describes yellow discoloration of the feet. It is an approved food coloring in the US and E100 in the EU.
